newsitem.title: UK: UK ad industry shrugs off Labour Party comments.
newsitem.headline: UK ad industry shrugs off Labour Party comments.

text.p: The British advertising industry on Thursday shrugged off a report that the Labour Party plans to tighten the regulation of advertising if it wins the next election, including imposing fines on advertisers that breach the industry's code of practice.

The trade publication Campaign on Thursday said Nigel Griffiths, Labour's shadow consumer affairs minister, disclosed plans to beef up the Advertising Standards Authority and impose fines on so-called "bad" advertisers. Griffiths is reviewing the party's policy on advertising.

"There are already statutory powers of that type to (handle) persistent wrongdoers," Lionel Stanbrook, deputy director general of the Advertising Association, told Reuters. The association, a federation of 27 trade associations and professional groups, represents advertisers, agencies, media and support services for an industry worth 10 billion pounds.
"We're in a very tightly regulated system already, and it's a system, thank God, that works," said Stanbrook.

The Labour Party has already started soliciting comments from the advertising industry on how it should be regulated, starting with a letter sent by Griffiths in late August to more than 1,000 people. Stanbrook said the Advertising Association and other industry groups are to meet with Griffiths on October 14.
"In four days we are going to talk to Nigel Griffiths about the best way to regulate the advertising industry," he said. "We're looking foward to a long, productive meeting on October 14."
Stanbrook said the Labour Party's efforts to consult with the advertising industry bodes well. "I'm no longer scared about the prospect of a Labour victory," said Stanbrook.
"I genuinely think Labour wants a really effective solution, and a genuinely effective system probably means there is room for further simplification," he said.
The Conservative Party has been in power in Britain since 1979, and many people in the advertising industry have been worried any future Labour government would be "anti-advertising".

Britain's advertising industry is self-regulating, with the industry's Advertising Standard Authority setting the code of practice for non-broadcast advertising and overseeing compliance. The ASA aims to insure that advertisements are "legal, decent, honest and truthful".

The Labour Party, which has been leading the ruling Conservative Party by about 20 percentage points in polls, is expected to drop its 1992 general election pledge to impose a statutory code of advertising practice. A general election in Britain must be held by spring 1997.

Griffiths said he was starting "with a clean slate" and did not rule out legislation, Campaign reported. Griffiths said Labour aims to make the existing self-regulatory system work better, the paper said.
"There is a problem with repeat offenders," Griffiths told Campaign. "Some people are making a career out of it."

Griffiths said he favours fining advertisers who repeatedly breach the code. Advertisers who continue to transgress after being fined could be banned from advertising the product or even banned from trading altogether, Campaign reported.
